1: # Audio Production — StickmanInkExplainer
2: 
3: > **Skill file for AI-assisted audio production.**
4: > Any AI reading this document should be able to produce broadcast-ready audio for a StickmanInkExplainer video from script to final master.
5: 
6: ---
7: 
8: ## 1 · Context
9: 
10: **Channel:** StickmanInkExplainer — Animated whiteboard explainer videos (Tech / Science / History / How Things Work).
11: **Audience:** English-speaking 16-35 (US/UK/AU/CA). **Upload cadence:** every 3-4 days. **Video length:** 3-8 min.
12: 
13: ### Audio Philosophy
14: 
15: > **Audio carries 80-90 % of the emotional weight in every StickmanInkExplainer video.**
16: > The visuals are clean and minimalist (white canvas, handwritten fonts). That means audio is what sells the story — the narrator's voice, the timing of a bass boom, the silence before a reveal. A viewer can glance away from the screen and still be hooked if the audio is right. If the audio is wrong, no amount of visual polish will save the video.
17: 
18: **Core principles:**
19: 
20: 1. **Voice is king** — the narrator is a calm, authoritative guide. Never a hype-man.
21: 2. **Music is subliminal** — the viewer should *feel* it without *noticing* it.
22: 3. **SFX sell the visuals** — every text pop, every scene cut, every reveal is punctuated by sound.
23: 4. **Ambient sets the world** — crackling fire for ancient scenes, fluorescent buzz for modern office.
24: 5. **Silence is a weapon** — a 1-1.5 s audio dropout before a big reveal hits harder than any boom.
25: 
26: ---
27: 
28: ## 2 · The 5 Audio Layers
29: 
30: Every finished StickmanInkExplainer video contains **exactly 5 audio layers**. No exceptions.
31: 
32: | # | Layer | Perceived Volume | dB Level | Role |
33: |---|-------|-----------------|----------|------|
34: | 1 | **Voiceover** | 100 % | 0 dB (reference) | Primary content delivery |
35: | 2 | **Background Music** | 12 % | -18 dB | Emotional undertone, mood shaping |
36: | 3 | **Sound Effects (SFX)** | 40 % | -8 dB | Punctuation of visual events |
37: | 4 | **Ambient Sounds** | 8-10 % | -20 dB | Scene-setting, world building |
38: | 5 | **Strategic Silence** | 0 % | -∞ dB | Complete audio dropout 1-1.5 s before reveals |
39: 
40: ### Layer interaction rules
41: 
42: - **Voice + Music** play simultaneously for ~85 % of the video.
43: - **SFX** are point events — short bursts overlaid on voice + music.
44: - **Ambient** is a continuous bed that runs under voice + music for scene-specific sections.
45: - **Strategic Silence** means ALL layers drop out (voice, music, SFX, ambient) for 1-1.5 seconds. Use at least 3 times per video, always before the biggest reveals.
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 3 · Voiceover Specification
50: 
51: ### 3.1 Voice Character
52: 
53: | Attribute | Target | Anti-target |
54: |-----------|--------|-------------|
55: | Tone | Calm, authoritative, slightly melancholic | Excited YouTuber, monotone robot, hyped influencer |
56: | Accent | American English (General American) | British RP, heavy regional accents |
57: | Pace | Variable — adapts to content | One fixed speed throughout |
58: | Emotion | Controlled — never breaks character | Over-the-top reactions, fake surprise |
59: | Feel | Documentary narrator who cares about the subject | News anchor reading a prompter |
60: 
61: Think: **David Attenborough meets Vsauce meets a campfire storyteller.**
62: 
63: ### 3.2 The 4 Voice Modes
64: 
65: > [!IMPORTANT]
66: > **ElevenLabs v3 — Emotional Tags Only.** We use emotional tags exclusively for voice direction — ignore Stability, Similarity, Style, and Speed sliders entirely. Emotional tags provide better, more consistent narrative control for our workflow. Prepend the matching emotional tag description to each script section before generating.
67: 
68: Switch between these modes based on script section type:
69: 
70: | Mode | When to Use | Speed | Pitch | Energy | ElevenLabs v3 Emotional Tag |
71: |------|------------|-------|-------|--------|-----------------------------|
72: | **Storytelling** | Default narration, scene-setting, context | Medium (140-155 WPM) | Natural mid-range | Warm, steady | `<emotional_tag>Speak in a warm, calm, and steady documentary narration style. Natural mid-range pitch. Even pacing with gentle emphasis on key words.</emotional_tag>` |
73: | **Building Tension** | Escalation, countdown progression, danger rising | Faster (155-175 WPM) | Slightly rising | Urgent but controlled | `<emotional_tag>Speak with rising urgency and controlled intensity. Slightly faster pace, pitch climbing subtly. Convey escalating danger while remaining grounded and authoritative.</emotional_tag>` |
74: | **The Reveal** | Major reveals, plot twists, "here's what actually happened" | Slower (110-130 WPM) | Lower, more deliberate | Measured, dramatic pauses | `<emotional_tag>Speak slowly and deliberately with dramatic weight. Lower pitch, measured pacing, significant pauses between phrases. Each word should land with gravity and importance.</emotional_tag>` |
75: | **Conversational** | Direct-to-viewer moments, "you" hooks, rhetorical questions | Casual (145-160 WPM) | Natural, relaxed | Like talking to a friend | `<emotional_tag>Speak in a relaxed, intimate conversational tone — like talking directly to a close friend. Natural pitch, casual pacing, warm and approachable.</emotional_tag>` |
76: 
77: ### 3.3 Section-by-Section Generation Workflow
78: 
79: > **CRITICAL: Generate voiceover in SECTIONS, never as one long take.**
80: 
81: **Why:** ElevenLabs produces more natural results when given shorter, focused segments. Long inputs cause drift — the voice becomes flatter, more robotic, and loses emotional variation. Shorter sections also let you prepend mode-specific emotional tags per segment for precise tonal control.
82: 
83: **Workflow:**
84: 
85: 1. **Split script into sections** — each section is 2-6 sentences, grouped by voice mode.
86: 2. **Tag each section** with its voice mode (Storytelling / Building Tension / The Reveal / Conversational).
87: 3. **Prepend the matching emotional tag** from the Voice Modes table (§ 3.2) to the section text.
88: 4. **Generate each section separately** in ElevenLabs with its emotional tag.
89: 5. **Review each section** — listen for robotic lines, unnatural cadence, mispronunciations.
90: 6. **Re-generate problem lines** — isolate the bad sentence, refine the emotional tag wording (e.g., add "more solemn" or "slightly brighter"), regenerate.
91: 6. **Export each section** as a separate WAV file (44.1 kHz, 16-bit minimum; 48 kHz, 24-bit preferred).
92: 7. **Insert 1-2 second silence** between sections during assembly (not in the TTS generation).
93: 
94: **File naming convention:**
95: 
96: ```
97: voiceover/
98: └── [video_slug]/
99:     ├── section_01_hook.wav          ← "You" hook, conversational mode
100:     ├── section_02_context.wav       ← Scene-setting, storytelling mode
101:     ├── section_03_escalation.wav    ← Building tension mode
102:     ├── section_04_reveal.wav        ← The reveal mode
103:     ├── section_05_list_block.wav    ← List items, building tension
104:     ├── section_06_philosophy.wav    ← Reflection, storytelling mode
105:     ├── section_07_callback.wav      ← Final callback, conversational
106:     └── section_08_cta.wav           ← Call to action, conversational
107: ```
108: 
109: ### 3.4 Detecting & Fixing Robotic Lines
110: 
111: Common signs of robotic TTS output and how to fix them:
112: 
113: | Problem | Symptom | Fix |
114: |---------|---------|-----|
115: | Flat delivery | No pitch variation across a sentence | Add more expressive language to the emotional tag (e.g., "with rising emotion", "passionately") |
116: | Over-emphasis | Weird stress on wrong syllables | Soften the emotional tag (e.g., "calmly", "with even pacing", "restrained") |
117: | Run-on phrasing | No natural pauses between clauses | Add punctuation — em dashes, ellipses, periods — to force pauses |
118: | Mispronunciation | Name/word mangled | Use phonetic spelling in the input: "Diocletian" → "Dye-oh-KLEE-shun" |
119: | Trailing mumble | End of sentence trails off | Add a period and a short follow-up sentence, then trim the extra audio |
120: | Identical cadence | Every sentence sounds the same | Break into smaller sections; vary sentence length and emotional tag per section |
121: | Breath artifacts | Unnatural gasps between words | Use audio editor to manually remove; or add "smooth and controlled breathing" to the emotional tag |
122: 
123: **The "Listen Test":** Play the generated audio while doing something else (scrolling, making coffee). If any line pulls you out of the experience — that line is robotic. Regenerate it.
124: 
125: ---
126: 
127: ## 4 · ElevenLabs Voice Selection Criteria
128: 
129: ### 4.1 What to Look For
130: 
131: | Criterion | Ideal | Avoid |
132: |-----------|-------|-------|
133: | Depth | Baritone to low tenor | High/thin voices |
134: | Naturalness | Sounds like a real human recording | Obvious AI artifacts |
135: | Warmth | Inviting, trustworthy | Cold, clinical |
136: | Control | Handles varied emotional tags consistently | Inconsistent across different emotional directions |
137: | Versatility | Handles both fast lists and slow reveals | Only sounds good at one speed |
138: 
139: ### 4.2 Recommended Voice Search Strategy
140: 
141: 1. **ElevenLabs Voice Library** — search with tags: `male`, `narration`, `documentary`, `calm`, `deep`.
142: 2. **Pre-made voices to audition** — try: `Adam`, `Antoni`, `Arnold`, `Clyde`, `Daniel`, `Dave`, `Fin`, `Josh`.
143: 3. **Voice Cloning** (if using Professional plan) — clone from royalty-free documentary narration samples.
144: 4. **Model selection** — use `eleven_multilingual_v2` or `eleven_turbo_v2_5` for best quality. Avoid older `v1` models.
145: 
146: ### 4.3 Emotional Tag Quick-Reference (ElevenLabs v3)
147: 
148: > [!NOTE]
149: > We use emotional tags exclusively — ignore Stability / Similarity / Style / Speed sliders. Prepend the tag below to the script text for each section.
150: 
151: | Section Type | ElevenLabs v3 Emotional Tag |
152: |-------------|-----------------------------|
153: | Hook (first 3 sec) | `<emotional_tag>Speak with confident, conversational energy — warm and engaging, like pulling someone into a story. Moderate pace.</emotional_tag>` |
154: | Storytelling | `<emotional_tag>Speak in a warm, calm, and steady documentary narration style. Natural mid-range pitch. Even pacing with gentle emphasis on key words.</emotional_tag>` |
155: | Building Tension | `<emotional_tag>Speak with rising urgency and controlled intensity. Slightly faster pace, pitch climbing subtly. Convey escalating danger while remaining grounded and authoritative.</emotional_tag>` |
156: | The Reveal | `<emotional_tag>Speak slowly and deliberately with dramatic weight. Lower pitch, measured pacing, significant pauses between phrases. Each word should land with gravity and importance.</emotional_tag>` |
157: | Conversational | `<emotional_tag>Speak in a relaxed, intimate conversational tone — like talking directly to a close friend. Natural pitch, casual pacing, warm and approachable.</emotional_tag>` |
158: | List entry call-out | `<emotional_tag>Speak with punchy, assertive emphasis on each item. Slightly faster pace, clear enunciation, controlled energy that builds with each entry.</emotional_tag>` |
159: | CTA (subscribe) | `<emotional_tag>Speak warmly and sincerely, like personally thanking a friend. Slightly slower, genuine, not salesy. Gentle and resolved.</emotional_tag>` |
160: 
161: > [!TIP]
162: > **Refining emotional tags:** If a line sounds flat, add more expressive descriptors (e.g., "with rising emotion", "passionately"). If it sounds chaotic or over-the-top, soften the tag (e.g., "calmly", "with restraint"). Small wording changes produce significant tonal shifts.
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## 5 · Background Music Rules
167: 
168: ### 5.1 Volume & Presence
169: 
170: - **Volume: 12 % perceived / -18 dB** relative to voiceover.
171: - The music should be **subliminal** — the viewer feels the mood without consciously hearing a track.
172: - If you can hum the melody while watching, the music is **too loud**.
173: - Music must **never** compete with voice for spectral space. Avoid music with vocals, prominent mid-range melodies, or sharp transients.
174: 
175: ### 5.2 Style Palette
176: 
177: | Script Mood | Music Style | Instruments | Tempo |
178: |-------------|-------------|-------------|-------|
179: | Neutral / context | Soft synth pads, lo-fi ambient | Pad synths, filtered piano | 60-80 BPM |
180: | Tense / dangerous | Dark ambient, minor-key drones | Sub-bass, distorted pads, sparse percussion | 70-100 BPM |
181: | Philosophical / reflective | Acoustic strings, melancholic piano | Solo cello, nylon guitar, Rhodes | 50-70 BPM |
182: | Escalation / countdown | Building percussive layers | Ticking percussion, rising synths | 90-120 BPM (accelerating) |
183: | Climax / peak reveal | Full swell — all elements hit | Orchestra hit + sub-bass + pad | Peaks then drops |
184: | Resolution / CTA | Warm, resolved, gentle | Acoustic guitar, warm pad | 60-80 BPM |
185: 
186: ### 5.3 Music Behavior Rules
187: 
188: 1. **Music CHANGES** with script sections — never use one track for the entire video.
189: 2. **Music swells** (increases 3-5 dB temporarily) at climax moments, then drops back.
190: 3. **Music DROPS to silence** 1-2 seconds before major reveals (part of strategic silence).
191: 4. **Crossfade between tracks** over 2-3 seconds when mood shifts.
192: 5. **Music fades in** at the start — don't start at full volume; 3-5 second fade-in.
193: 6. **Music fades out** at CTA — gentle 5-second fade to zero under final words.
194: 
195: ### 5.4 Sources (Copyright-Safe)
196: 
197: | Source | Cost | Quality | Notes |
198: |--------|------|---------|-------|
199: | **YouTube Audio Library** | Free | Good | Pre-cleared for YouTube; search by mood/genre |
200: | **Pixabay Music** | Free | Variable | CC0, no attribution required |
201: | **Epidemic Sound** | $15/mo | Excellent | Best variety; stems available for mixing |
202: | **Artlist** | $10/mo | Excellent | Unlimited license; great ambient selection |
203: | **Unminus** | Free | Good | Small but curated, all free |
204: 
205: > [!CAUTION]
206: > **NEVER use copyright-claimed music.** Even "royalty-free" tracks from random sites can trigger Content ID. Stick to the sources above. Always verify the license before using any track.
207: 
208: ---
209: 
210: ## 6 · SFX Library Specification
211: 
212: This is the **complete shopping list** of sound effects needed for StickmanInkExplainer videos. Download all of these before starting production.
213: 
214: | Category | Specific Sounds | Usage | Source | Files Needed |
215: |----------|----------------|-------|--------|-------------|
216: | **Transitions** | Soft whoosh, medium whoosh, hard whoosh, reverse whoosh | Every scene change / hard cut | Pixabay, Freesound | 4 files |
217: | **Text Impacts** | Marker squeak, pen scratch on paper, UI pop/click, digital blip | Every on-screen text appearance | Pixabay | 4-6 files |
218: | **Bass Hits** | Low sub-bass boom, impact thud, deep drum hit, cinematic hit | Before reveals, new list entries, stat displays | Freesound, Mixkit | 3-4 files |
219: | **Ambient Ancient** | Fire crackling, wind howling, rain on stone, night forest, river flowing, torch flame | Ancient/historical scenes | BBC Sound Effects, Freesound | 6+ files |
220: | **Ambient Modern** | City traffic, phone notification, keyboard typing, fluorescent buzz, office hum, crowd murmur | Modern-day scenes | Freesound, Pixabay | 6+ files |
221: | **Dramatic** | Heartbeat (slow), heartbeat (fast), tension riser, suspense drone, stinger hit | Building to climax, emotional peaks | Mixkit, Freesound | 5 files |
222: | **Silence** | Clean digital silence — 1 s and 2 s versions | Before important reveals, between sections | **Create yourself** (see below) | 2 files |
223: | **Visceral** | Bone crack, water splash, chain rattle, rat squeak, metal scrape, whip crack | Survival content, punishment, physical scenarios | Freesound | 6+ files |
224: | **Red X Mark** | Sharp marker squeak / dry-erase on whiteboard | When crossing out concepts, debunking | Pixabay | 1-2 files |
225: | **UI / Digital** | Notification ding, error buzz, progress tick, cash register | Stats, numbers, modern references | Pixabay | 4 files |
226: | **Nature** | Thunder crack, earthquake rumble, wave crash, bird calls | Environmental establishing shots | BBC Sound Effects | 4-6 files |
227: 
228: ### Creating Silence Files
229: 
230: Generate clean silence with FFMPEG — do NOT use recordings (they contain noise):
231: 
232: ```bash
233: # 1-second silence (48 kHz, stereo, 24-bit)
234: ffmpeg -f lavfi -i anullsrc=r=48000:cl=stereo -t 1.0 -c:a pcm_s24le audio/sfx/silence/silence_1s.wav
235: 
236: # 1.5-second silence
237: ffmpeg -f lavfi -i anullsrc=r=48000:cl=stereo -t 1.5 -c:a pcm_s24le audio/sfx/silence/silence_1500ms.wav
238: 
239: # 2-second silence
240: ffmpeg -f lavfi -i anullsrc=r=48000:cl=stereo -t 2.0 -c:a pcm_s24le audio/sfx/silence/silence_2s.wav
241: ```
242: 
243: ---
244: 
245: ## 7 · SFX Timing Rules
246: 
247: ### 7.1 Sync Principles
248: 
249: | Rule | Detail |
250: |------|--------|
251: | **SFX syncs to visuals** | Every SFX is tied to a visual event — never free-floating. |
252: | **Visual appears 5-10 frames AFTER the spoken word** | The narrator says "death" → 5-10 frames later (0.17-0.33 s at 30 fps) the text "DEATH" appears on screen with its SFX. |
253: | **Hard cut SFX on FIRST FRAME** | When cutting to a new scene, the whoosh/boom lands exactly on frame 1 of the new shot. |
254: | **Text impact SFX on text appearance frame** | The marker squeak / UI pop plays on the exact frame the text element appears. |
255: | **Bass boom on every new list number** | In countdown/list videos, each new number (5… 4… 3…) gets a bass hit. |
256: | **Red X = marker squeak** | Every time a concept is crossed out with a red X, play the dry-erase marker squeak. |
257: | **Strategic silence = ALL layers drop** | 1-1.5 s before the biggest reveals, ALL audio drops to zero. Then the reveal line hits. |
258: 
259: ### 7.2 Strategic Silence Protocol
260: 
261: **When to deploy (minimum 3 per video):**
262: 
263: 1. Before the **single biggest reveal** of the video (e.g., "the real reason is…")
264: 2. Before the **#1 entry** in a list/countdown
265: 3. Before the **final philosophical statement** or callback
266: 
267: **How to implement:**
268: 
269: 1. Fade ALL audio layers to zero over 0.3 seconds.
270: 2. Hold complete silence for 1.0-1.5 seconds.
271: 3. The reveal line begins — voice returns at full volume, music at half volume, then music fades back to normal over 2 seconds.
272: 
273: ### 7.3 Timing Offset Table
274: 
275: | Event | SFX Timing | SFX Type |
276: |-------|-----------|----------|
277: | Scene cut (hard cut) | Frame 0 of new scene | Whoosh (soft/medium/hard based on intensity) |
278: | Text appears on screen | Frame 0 of text appearance | Marker squeak OR UI pop |
279: | Stat number appears large | Frame 0 of number | Bass boom + UI pop |
280: | List entry number | On the vocal emphasis of the number | Bass boom |
281: | Red X crosses out text | Frame 0 of X animation | Marker squeak |
282: | Reveal moment | After 1-1.5 s silence | Bass boom (heavy) |
283: | Danger mentioned | 5-10 frames after spoken word | Tension riser (subtle) |
284: | End card / CTA | Background only | Soft UI ding |
285: 
286: ---
287: 
288: ## 8 · FFMPEG Audio Mixing Commands
289: 
290: ### 8.1 Production Pipeline: 2-Pass Approach
291: 
292: > **Pass 1:** Mix all audio layers into a single master audio file.
293: > **Pass 2:** Combine master audio with assembled visuals into final export.
294: 
295: This 2-pass approach lets you perfect the audio independently and catch problems before the expensive video encode.
296: 
297: ### 8.2 Concatenating Voiceover Sections
298: 
299: First, join all voiceover sections into a single continuous voiceover track:
300: 
301: ```bash
302: # Create a file list for concatenation
303: # concat_list.txt contains:
304: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_01_hook.wav'
305: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_02_context.wav'
306: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_03_escalation.wav'
307: # ... etc.
308: 
309: ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i concat_list.txt -c:a pcm_s24le voiceover_full.wav
310: ```
311: 
312: To insert silence between sections during concatenation:
313: 
314: ```bash
315: # Build concat_list_with_gaps.txt:
316: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_01_hook.wav'
317: # file 'audio/sfx/silence/silence_1s.wav'
318: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_02_context.wav'
319: # file 'audio/sfx/silence/silence_1500ms.wav'
320: # file 'voiceover/video_slug/section_03_escalation.wav'
321: # ... etc.
322: 
323: ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i concat_list_with_gaps.txt -c:a pcm_s24le voiceover_full.wav
324: ```
325: 
326: ### 8.3 Volume Adjustment Per Layer
327: 
328: Individual layer volume commands for reference:
329: 
330: ```bash
331: # Voiceover — 0 dB (no change, reference level)
332: ffmpeg -i voiceover_full.wav -af "volume=1.0" -c:a pcm_s24le vo_leveled.wav
333: 
334: # Background Music — -18 dB
335: ffmpeg -i music_track.wav -af "volume=-18dB" -c:a pcm_s24le music_leveled.wav
336: 
337: # SFX — -8 dB
338: ffmpeg -i sfx_track.wav -af "volume=-8dB" -c:a pcm_s24le sfx_leveled.wav
339: 
340: # Ambient — -20 dB
341: ffmpeg -i ambient_track.wav -af "volume=-20dB" -c:a pcm_s24le ambient_leveled.wav
342: ```
343: 
344: ### 8.4 Music Fade In / Fade Out
345: 
346: ```bash
347: # Fade in over 3 seconds at start, fade out over 5 seconds ending at 540s (9 min mark)
348: ffmpeg -i music_track.wav -af "afade=t=in:st=0:d=3,afade=t=out:st=535:d=5,volume=-18dB" music_faded.wav
349: ```
350: 
351: ### 8.5 Music Swell at Climax
352: 
353: ```bash
354: # Music at -18 dB normally, swells to -12 dB from 360s to 375s, then back to -18 dB
355: ffmpeg -i music_track.wav -af "volume=-18dB,volume=enable='between(t,360,375)':volume=6dB" music_swell.wav
356: ```
357: 
358: ### 8.6 Time-Offsetting SFX with adelay
359: 
360: ```bash
361: # Delay an SFX by 45.5 seconds (45500 ms) — e.g., a bass boom at the 45.5s mark
362: ffmpeg -i bass_boom.wav -af "adelay=45500|45500" bass_boom_delayed.wav
363: 
364: # Multiple SFX at different timestamps — merge them into one SFX track
365: ffmpeg \
366:   -i bass_boom.wav \
367:   -i whoosh_medium.wav \
368:   -i marker_squeak.wav \
369:   -filter_complex "\
370:     [0:a]adelay=45500|45500,volume=-8dB[sfx1]; \
371:     [1:a]adelay=52000|52000,volume=-8dB[sfx2]; \
372:     [2:a]adelay=52200|52200,volume=-8dB[sfx3]; \
373:     [sfx1][sfx2][sfx3]amix=inputs=3:duration=longest:dropout_transition=0[sfx_mix]" \
374:   -map "[sfx_mix]" -c:a pcm_s24le sfx_composite.wav
375: ```
376: 
377: ### 8.7 Full 5-Layer Master Audio Mix
378: 
379: This is the **primary mixing command** — it combines all 5 layers into one master audio file:
380:

61: ### Step 1: Data Gathering
62: 
63: **Goal**: Collect 30-50 raw facts, studies, historical events, and data points. Quantity over quality at this stage — you'll filter later.
64: 
65: **What to look for**:
66: 
67: | Category | What It Means | Example |
68: |---|---|---|
69: | Scientific studies | Peer-reviewed research with named authors | "Dr. Roger Ekirch, Virginia Tech, 2001 — discovered 'biphasic sleep' in pre-industrial humans" |
70: | Counter-intuitive findings | Facts that contradict common assumptions | "Ancient humans were taller than medieval Europeans" |
71: | Historical anchors | Specific dates, events, named people | "In 1347, the Black Death reached Sicily via Genoese ships from Caffa" |
72: | Psychological hooks | Why the brain cares about this topic | "Your fear of the dark isn't irrational — it's a 200,000-year-old survival instinct" |
73: | Modern parallels | Ancient behavior mirrored today | "Homo erectus controlled fire → you check your phone 96 times a day (same dopamine loop)" |
74: | Surprising statistics | Numbers that provoke a reaction | "99.9% of all species that ever lived are now extinct" |
75: 
76: **Where to search (in order of priority)**:
77: 
78: 1. Google Scholar — search `[topic] study site:scholar.google.com`
79: 2. PubMed — for psychology, neuroscience, biology
80: 3. JSTOR / ResearchGate — for historical and anthropological studies
81: 4. Nature, Science, PNAS — flagship journals
82: 5. Science journalism — New Scientist, Scientific American, Ars Technica, Quanta Magazine
83: 6. Primary historical sources — translated texts, archaeological reports
84: 7. Reputable books — authors who are active researchers in the field

86: ### Step 2: Structuring
87: 
88: **Goal**: Organize raw facts into a narrative arc. The StickmanInkExplainer script structure follows:
89: 
90: ```
91: Hook → Context → Evidence → Twist → Reflection
92: ```
93: 
94: | Arc Stage | Purpose | Research Needed |
95: |---|---|---|
96: | **Hook** | Grab attention in first 3 seconds | 1 shocking fact or "you" statement |
97: | **Context** | Why does this topic exist? | Historical timeline, origin story |
98: | **Evidence** | The meat — studies, data, examples | 5-10 sourced facts, escalating intensity |
99: | **Twist** | The counter-intuitive reveal | 1-2 findings that flip the narrative |
100: | **Reflection** | Why it matters to the viewer | Modern parallel, emotional connection |
101: 
102: At this stage, discard any facts that:
103: - Don't fit the narrative arc
104: - Can't be sourced to a named researcher, institution, or historical record
105: - Are commonly known and won't surprise the audience
106: - Don't connect emotionally to the viewer's life

108: ### Step 3: Insight Mining
109: 
110: **Goal**: Identify the ONE unique angle — the thesis that makes THIS video different from every other video on the same topic.
111: 
112: **Process**:
113: 1. Search YouTube for existing videos on the topic
114: 2. Watch/skim the top 5 results — note what angles they use
115: 3. Ask: "What did NONE of them cover?"
116: 4. That gap is your angle
117: 5. Express it in ONE sentence
118: 
119: **Example**:
120: - Topic: "Ancient human sleep"
121: - Existing videos cover: "Humans used to sleep more," "Blue light ruins sleep," "Polyphasic sleep"
122: - Gap found: Nobody covers that pre-industrial humans had **two separate sleep periods** with a waking hour of prayer, sex, and reflection in between
123: - Unique angle: **"Ancient humans had TWO sleep periods per night — and the hour between them might be the key to creativity"**
124: - This is exactly what made ThePaintExplainer's videos go viral

313: ## 5. The "Unique Angle" Framework
314: 
315: The unique angle is the single most important output of the research process. Without it, you have a Wikipedia summary. With it, you have a viral video.
316: 
317: ### The 4-Step Angle Discovery Process
318: 
319: ```
320: 1. SEARCH  →  YouTube search for "[TOPIC]", note top 10 videos
321: 2. MAP     →  What angle does each video take? List them.
322: 3. GAP     →  What angle has NOT been covered?
323: 4. VALIDATE →  Does this gap have demand? (Would people click?)
324: ```
325: 
326: ### Decision Tree
327: 
328: ```
329: Found a gap in existing coverage?
330: ├── YES → Does the angle trigger emotion? (curiosity/shock/fear/awe)
331: │   ├── YES → Can you express it in ONE sentence?
332: │   │   ├── YES → ✅ You have your unique angle
333: │   │   └── NO  → The angle is too vague. Narrow it down.
334: │   └── NO  → Find a more emotionally resonant sub-angle
335: └── NO  → The topic is oversaturated
336:     ├── Can you find a SUB-TOPIC within it?
337:     │   ├── YES → Repeat the process for the sub-topic
338:     │   └── NO  → ❌ Abandon this topic. Pick a new one.
339:     └── Can you combine it with an unrelated field?
340:         ├── YES → "What if [TOPIC A] meets [TOPIC B]?" — test this angle
341:         └── NO  → ❌ Abandon this topic.
342: ```

491:

494: | Dimension | 💀 DEAD Research | 🔥 ALIVE Research |
495: |---|---|---|
496: | **Sources** | "Scientists say..." / "Studies show..." | "Dr. Dayu Lin at NYU found in a 2013 study published in *Nature*..." |
497: | **Facts** | Generic, widely known | Counter-intuitive, surprising, specific |

501: | **Timeline** | No historical context | Deep timeline (1,000-200,000 years) |
502: | **Modern Connection** | "This is interesting" | "This is why YOU do [specific behavior] every day" |

462: def analyze_speaking_pace(output_dir):

472:         segments = json.load(f)
473: 
474:     if not segments:
475:         return None
476: 
477:     # Group words/segments into 30-second buckets
478:     BUCKET_SIZE = 30  # seconds
479:     buckets = {}
480:     
481:     for seg in segments:
482:         start = seg.get('start', 0)
483:         text = seg.get('text', '')
484:         bucket_idx = int(start // BUCKET_SIZE)
485:         
486:         if bucket_idx not in buckets:
487:             buckets[bucket_idx] = {'words': 0, 'start': bucket_idx * BUCKET_SIZE}
488:         buckets[bucket_idx]['words'] += len(text.split())
489: 
490:     # Calculate WPM per bucket
491:     pace_data = []
492:     for idx in sorted(buckets.keys()):
493:         b = buckets[idx]
494:         wpm = (b['words'] / BUCKET_SIZE) * 60
495:         pace_data.append({
496:             'section': idx + 1,
497:             'time_range': f"{format_seconds(b['start'])} - {format_seconds(b['start'] + BUCKET_SIZE)}",
498:             'word_count': b['words'],
499:             'wpm': round(wpm, 1),
500:             'pace': 'SLOW' if wpm < 120 else 'NORMAL' if wpm < 170 else 'FAST'
501:         })

503:     # Summary stats
504:     all_wpm = [p['wpm'] for p in pace_data if p['wpm'] > 0]
505:     summary = {
506:         'sections': pace_data,
507:         'average_wpm': round(sum(all_wpm) / len(all_wpm), 1) if all_wpm else 0,
508:         'min_wpm': round(min(all_wpm), 1) if all_wpm else 0,
509:         'max_wpm': round(max(all_wpm), 1) if all_wpm else 0,
510:         'pace_variation': round(max(all_wpm) - min(all_wpm), 1) if all_wpm else 0,
511:     }

513:     pace_path = os.path.join(output_dir, 'speaking_pace.json')
514:     with open(pace_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:

518:     print(f"  ✅ Range: {summary['min_wpm']} - {summary['max_wpm']} WPM")
519:     print(f"  ✅ Pace variation: {summary['pace_variation']} WPM")

379: ## 4. Hook Engineering — The First 15 Seconds
380: 
381: > **The Rule:** 55% of viewers decide to stay or leave in the first 15 seconds. The hook is the most important part of the script. No intro. No logo. No "hey guys." Cold open ONLY.
382: 
383: ### 5 Proven Hook Types
384: 
385: #### Type 1: "You" Scenario Hook ⭐ (Highest performing)
386: Places the viewer directly into the situation. Creates immediate empathy.
387: 
388: > **Example (Zenn, 7.4M views):** "You're lying in bed right now, scrolling through your phone at 2 AM. The glow of the screen is the only light in the room. But for 300,000 years, when the sun went down, there was nothing."
389: 
390: > **Example (AxenCool, 2M views):** "You wake up. You check your phone. You drag yourself to a job you're not sure you care about. You sit in traffic. You eat something fast. You come home exhausted."
391: 
392: > **Formula:** "You [sensory action in present tense]. You [second detail]. [Contrast or twist]."
393: 
394: #### Type 2: Shocking Stat Hook
395: Leads with a number so extreme it forces attention.
396: 
397: > **Example (SimplePaint style):** "In 1999, a man received 17 sieverts of radiation. The fatal dose is 8. He was kept alive for 83 days."
398: 
399: > **Example (Infographics Show):** "Every 60 seconds, your body produces 3.8 million cells. And right now, at least one of them is trying to kill you."
400: 
401: > **Formula:** "[Specific number + context]. [Why that number is terrifying/fascinating]."
402: 
403: #### Type 3: Teaser + Pullback Hook
404: Shows the climax, then rewinds to the beginning.
405: 
406: > **Example (GoodEnoughAnimation style):** "There is one place on Earth where the human body dissolves in under 30 minutes. But let's not start there. Let's start with something milder."
407: 
408: > **Example:** "The last thing he saw was his own skeleton. Through his hands. But to understand how he got there, we need to go back six hours."
409: 
410: > **Formula:** "[The most extreme moment in the video, one sentence]. [Pull back]. [Promise to explain how we get there]."
411: 
412: #### Type 4: "What If" Scenario Hook
413: Poses a hypothetical that triggers curiosity.
414: 
415: > **Example (Pursuit of Wonder, 11M views):** "What if you stopped sleeping? Not gradually — just stopped, completely, right now. What happens next isn't gradual. It's a cliff."
416: 
417: > **Example:** "What if every human on Earth suddenly lost the ability to feel pain? You might think that's a superpower. Within a week, it would be an extinction event."
418: 
419: > **Formula:** "What if [vivid hypothetical]? You might think [common assumption]. [Why the assumption is wrong]."
420: 
421: #### Type 5: Contrarian / Counter-Intuitive Hook
422: States something that feels wrong, forcing the viewer to stay and hear the explanation.
423: 
424: > **Example (Monkey Mind, 4.9M views):** "Your brain doesn't want you to be happy. That's not a metaphor. That's not pessimism. That's literally how your brain is designed."
425: 
426: > **Example:** "Boredom is the most dangerous emotion a human can feel. Not anger. Not fear. Boredom. And there's a body count to prove it."
427: 
428: > **Formula:** "[Counter-intuitive claim]. [Dismiss the obvious objection]. [Hint at evidence]."
429:

431: 
432: | Second | What Happens | Audio | Visual |
433: |---|---|---|---|
434: | 0-1 | First word spoken — mid-sentence energy, NO warm-up | Voice only, music barely fading in | 📸 First image — attention-grabbing, high contrast |
435: | 1-3 | Complete the opening "You" line or shocking stat | Voice + faint music bed | Same image or supporting visual |
436: | 3-5 | Second sentence — deepen the scenario | Music slightly louder | 📸 Second image — supporting detail |
437: | 5-7 | The TURN — "But..." / contrast / twist | 🔊 Subtle bass hit or mood shift | 📸 Contrasting image (mood change) |
438: | 7-10 | Expand on the contrast / open the loop | Music settling into tone | 📸 Image supporting the new direction |
439: | 10-12 | First micro-hook or question | Voice emphasis | 📸 Image change |

441: | 15-20 | First piece of context / data | Conversational pace | 📸 Visual supporting the data |

445: ### Hook Score Rubric (Rate 1-10)
446: 
447: Use this rubric to evaluate any hook before finalizing it:
448: 
449: | Criterion | 0 Points | 1 Point | 2 Points |
450: |---|---|---|---|
451: | **Immediacy** | Slow buildup, throat-clearing | Gets to the point in 2-3 sentences | First sentence is the hook itself |
452: | **Emotion** | No emotional trigger | Mild curiosity | Visceral reaction (shock, fear, wonder, "wait what?") |
453: | **Open Loop** | No unanswered question | Vague promise of more info | Specific question planted that MUST be answered |
454: | **Visual Potential** | Abstract, hard to visualize | Can picture a general scene | Specific, vivid image forms in the mind immediately |

466: 
467: Embed these markers directly in the script text. They tell the voiceover engineer, image generator, and video editor exactly what to do at each moment.

469: ### Marker Reference
470: 
471: | Marker | Meaning | Effect on Production |
472: |---|---|---|
473: | 🔥 | **High energy** — slightly faster voice pace | VO: +5-10% speed. Music: +2dB. Cuts: faster (2-3s holds) |
474: | ⏸️ | **Pause** — 1-2 seconds of silence after this line | VO: stop speaking. Music: continue soft. SFX: none. |
475: | 🔇 | **Quiet / slow** — let the words sink in | VO: -10% speed, softer. Music: -3dB or drop out. Cuts: slower (5-8s holds) |
476: | ❗ | **Emphasis** — stress this word/phrase | VO: slightly louder on marked word. May add text overlay on screen. |
477: | 🎵 | **Music mood change** | Editor: crossfade to new track or shift intensity |
478: | 🔊 | **SFX cue** — trigger a sound effect | Editor: insert specified SFX at this timestamp |
479: | 📸 | **New visual** — image/scene change here | Editor: cut to new image. Include brief description after marker. |

582: ## 7. Language Rules
583: 
584: These rules are **non-negotiable**. Every script must follow them. They are the difference between a "dead" script (reads like Wikipedia) and an "alive" script (feels like someone talking to you).
585: 
586: ### Rule 1: Maximum 15 Words Per Sentence for Impact Lines
587: 
588: Impact lines are revelations, twists, key facts, and emotional peaks. They must be short.
589: 
590: > ❌ "The process of dopamine regulation in the prefrontal cortex involves a complex interplay of neurotransmitter reuptake mechanisms that were originally evolved for survival purposes."
591: >
592: > ✅ "Your brain wasn't built for this. It was built for berries and bears."
593: 
594: Exposition lines (bridges, context) can be longer — up to 25 words. But impact lines: 15 words max.
595: 
596: ### Rule 2: "You" as Primary Perspective
597: 
598: Target: **40+ uses of "you/your/you're" per 10-minute script.**
599: 
600: > ❌ "People often find themselves unable to focus in the modern world."
601: > ✅ "You can't focus. And it's not your fault."
602: 
603: > ❌ "Ancient humans experienced different sleep patterns."
604: > ✅ "Your ancestors slept differently than you do. Radically differently."
605: 
606: ### Rule 3: Questions Every 60-90 Seconds
607: 
608: Target: **8-15 questions per script.** Mix rhetorical questions ("So why does this happen?") with direct questions ("What would you do?").
609: 
610: Placement: After every major information block. The question gives the viewer's brain a moment to process AND creates a reason to keep watching for the answer.
611: 
612: ### Rule 4: Write for the EAR, Not the Eye
613: 
614: Read every line aloud. If you stumble, rewrite. If it sounds like an essay, rewrite.
615: 
616: **EAR words (use these):** "thing," "stuff," "weird," "wild," "basically," "look," "here's the deal," "right?", "turns out," "think about it"
617: 
618: **EYE words (avoid these):** "furthermore," "consequently," "thus," "regarding," "in terms of," "it should be noted that," "studies indicate," "one might argue"
619: 
620: ### Rule 5: Translate Data Into Feelings — Immediately
621: 
622: Never drop a statistic without immediately telling the viewer what it FEELS like.
623: 
624: > ❌ "The temperature reached 1,200 degrees Fahrenheit."
625: > ✅ "The temperature hit 1,200 degrees. That's hot enough to melt aluminum. Hot enough that the air itself starts to glow."
626: 
627: > ❌ "A study by Harvard in 2019 found that 73% of adults report feeling chronically stressed."
628: > ✅ "In 2019, Harvard ran a study. Nearly three out of four adults said they feel stressed — not sometimes — ❗ chronically. As in, it never stops."
629: 
630: ### Rule 6: Scientific Citations — Humanize Them
631: 
632: **Formula:** Researcher name + year + "what they found" in plain English + emotional translation.
633:

1: # Packaging & Validation — StickmanInkExplainer YouTube Channel
2: 
3: > **Purpose**: This file teaches any AI assistant how to validate video concepts, craft titles, design thumbnails, and ensure every video is worth producing BEFORE investing hours into scripting, image generation, and editing. This is the single most important step in the entire production pipeline.
4: 
5: ---
6: 
7: ## 1. Context
8: 
9: **Channel**: StickmanInkExplainer — AI-generated whiteboard explainer videos covering Tech / Science / History / How Things Work topics.
10: **Audience**: US/UK/AU/CA English speakers, ages 18–34.
11: **Format**: 8–12 minute videos, uploaded every 3 days.
12: **Visual Style**: Animated whiteboard explainer, white canvas, handwritten fonts, photorealistic images.
13: 
14: ### Why Packaging Is 70–80% of a Video's Success
15: 
16: A video with a perfect script, stunning visuals, and flawless audio will get **zero views** if nobody clicks on it. Packaging — the title + thumbnail combo — is the ONLY thing a viewer sees before deciding to click. YouTube's algorithm doesn't promote "good videos." It promotes videos that **get clicked** and **get watched**. The algorithm tests your video by showing it to a small sample. If that sample doesn't click, the video dies — no matter how good the content is.
17: 
18: **The math is brutal:**
19: - YouTube shows your thumbnail to ~500 people initially
20: - Average CTR for new channels: 2–5%
21: - A 2% CTR = 10 clicks from 500 impressions → video dies
22: - A 10% CTR = 50 clicks from 500 impressions → algorithm pushes harder
23: - The difference between 2% and 10% CTR is the difference between 1K views and 1M views
24: 
25: **This means**: You must obsess over packaging BEFORE you write a single word of script. If the title and thumbnail aren't irresistible, the video should never be made.
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ## 2. The Title-First Workflow (MrBeast Method)
30: 
31: This is the production workflow used by MrBeast, Ryan Trahan, Mark Rober, and virtually every creator who consistently gets millions of views. It is **NON-NEGOTIABLE** for the StickmanInkExplainer channel.
32: 
33: ### Step 1: Find Topic
34: - Browse competitors (ThePaintExplainer, Kurzgesagt, RealLifeLore, Lemmino)
35: - Look at trending topics in Tech / Science / History / How Things Work niches
36: - Check Reddit threads, Wikipedia rabbit holes, "how does it work" forums
37: - Track what's working RIGHT NOW — not what worked 2 years ago
38: 
39: ### Step 2: Write Title + Design Thumbnail Concept
40: - Before writing ANY script, write the title
41: - Sketch the thumbnail concept (what the viewer sees at 1.5cm × 0.8cm on mobile)
42: - The title and thumbnail must work TOGETHER — they are one unit, not two separate things
43: - The title says one thing, the thumbnail shows another → combined they create irresistible curiosity
44: 
45: ### Step 3: If You Can't Make Them Irresistible → THROW THE TOPIC AWAY
46: - If after 15 minutes you can't write a title that makes YOU want to click → kill the topic
47: - If you can't imagine a thumbnail that would stop YOUR scroll → kill the topic
48: - Do NOT fall in love with a topic. Fall in love with PACKAGING
49: - There are infinite topics. There are NOT infinite good titles
50: - **Sunk cost is zero at this stage** — you've invested nothing yet
51: 
52: ### Step 4: Only Then Write the Script
53: - Once you have a killer title + thumbnail concept, NOW write the script
54: - The script must deliver on the PROMISE of the title
55: - If the title says "Every Computer Component Explained" the script must deliver genuinely clear, thorough explanations of every major component
56: - Under-delivering on title promise = high CTR but low retention = algorithm punishes you
57: 
58: > [!CAUTION]
59: > **NEVER** write a script first and then try to reverse-engineer a title from it. This is the #1 mistake small creators make. It produces generic titles like "Computer Parts Overview" instead of "Every Computer Component Explained."
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 3. The 4-Step Validation System
64: 
65: Every topic must pass ALL four steps before it moves to scripting.
66: 
67: ### Step 1: "Proven Demand" Test
68: 
69: **Method**: Search the topic on YouTube. Look for small channels (under 100K subscribers) that got disproportionately high view counts on that topic.
70: 
71: **Why this works**: If a 5K-subscriber channel got 2M views on "What Did Ancient Humans Do at Night?" — that proves the TOPIC has demand, not the channel. The algorithm pushed it because people clicked and watched. If you can package it better, you can replicate or exceed those numbers.
72: 
73: **How to execute**:
74: 1. Search YouTube for your topic keywords
75: 2. Filter by "This month" or "This year" for freshness
76: 3. Look for videos with view-to-subscriber ratios of 10:1 or higher
77: 4. Document the exact title, view count, subscriber count, and upload date
78: 5. If you find 2+ examples of small channels getting 500K+ views → topic is VALIDATED
79: 
80: **Red flag**: If every video on the topic has under 100K views regardless of channel size, the topic has LOW DEMAND. Kill it.
81: 
82: **Examples of proven demand**:
83: 
84: | Topic | Video Title | Views | Channel Subs | Ratio |
85: |-------|-------------|-------|-------------|-------|
86: | Dying on planets | "What Dying on Every Planet Would Be Like" | 12M | ~200K | 60:1 |
87: | Human mistakes in history | "Every Major Human Mistake That Changed History" | 7.5M | ~150K | 50:1 |
88: | Worst punishments | "The Worst Punishments in History" | 8.7M | ~100K | 87:1 |
89: | Computer components | "Every Computer Component Explained" | 3M+ | ~80K | 37:1 |
90: | Ancient predators | "How Did Ancient Humans Survive the World's Deadliest Predators?" | 2M | ~30K | 66:1 |
91: 
92: ### Step 2: "Would I Click?" Test
93: 
94: **Method**: Imagine your title + thumbnail sitting between a MrBeast video and a Netflix recommendation in your feed. Would you GENUINELY click yours?
95: 
96: **Be brutally honest**. Not "would I click if I was bored" — would I click RIGHT NOW, with MrBeast offering "$1 vs $1,000,000 Hotel" right next to it?
97: 
98: **Checklist**:
99: - Does the title create an unanswered question in my mind? (Yes/No)
100: - Does the question feel URGENT to answer? (Yes/No)
101: - Would I feel like I'm MISSING OUT if I scrolled past? (Yes/No)
102: - Does the thumbnail make me feel something (curiosity, intrigue, fascination)? (Yes/No)
103: 
104: **All four must be YES.** If any is No, rework the title/thumbnail or kill the topic.
105: 
106: ### Step 3: "3 Variations" Rule
107: 
108: **Method**: Write at least 3 title variations for every topic. Never go with the first title you think of.
109: 
110: **Example — Topic: How computers actually process information**:
111: 
112: | Version | Title | Strength |
113: |---------|-------|----------|
114: | A | "How Computers Actually Work" | Clear, proven formula, but overused |
115: | B | "Every Computer Component Explained — From CPU to RAM" | Comprehensive, specific parts named |
116: | C | "How Your Computer Actually Works (You Use It Daily But Don't Know)" | Personal ("Your"), knowledge gap, daily relevance |
117: 
118: **Winner**: Version C — it puts YOU in the scenario, highlights the knowledge gap, and implies you should know this since you use it every day.
119: 
120: **How to pick the winner**:
121: 1. Which one creates the strongest emotional response?
122: 2. Which one is most specific (numbers, timeframes, named things)?
123: 3. Which one sounds DIFFERENT from existing videos on the topic?
124: 4. Which one works best WITH a thumbnail concept?
125: 
126: ### Step 4: "Thumbnail Scroll" Test
127: 
128: **Method**: Imagine your thumbnail as a tiny rectangle (roughly the size of your thumbnail on your phone — about 1.5cm wide). Can you still read the text? Can you still understand the key visual? Does it stand out from the sea of other thumbnails?
129: 
130: **Criteria**:
131: - Text is readable at mobile size (2–4 words MAX)
132: - Key visual that represents the topic is instantly clear
133: - Color contrast pops against YouTube's white/dark background
134: - The image raises a QUESTION — it doesn't answer one
135: - It looks DIFFERENT from the 10 thumbnails around it
136: 
137: **If you can't clearly describe the thumbnail in one sentence, it's too complex.** Simplify.

277: ## 6. Thumbnail Design Rules
278: 
279: ### Core Principles
280: 
281: 1. **High Contrast**: Bold elements on clean backgrounds. White/light background with dark text and vivid photorealistic visuals.
282: 2. **ONE Key Visual**: A single photorealistic image, product photo, diagram, or icon as the focal point. Not two, not three. ONE. The viewer's eye must go to one focal point.
283: 3. **2–4 Word Text**: Bold handwritten font (Patrick Hand or Impact style). If you need more than 4 words, you're saying too much.
284: 4. **Text Creates a QUESTION**: The text should make the viewer think "what does that mean?" — not provide an answer.
285: 5. **Mobile-First**: Design for mobile. If text isn't readable at thumbnail size on a phone, it fails.
286: 6. **1080p Resolution**: Always 1920 × 1080 (Remotion default). Clean and optimized for web delivery.
287: 
288: ### Layout Structure
289: 
290: ```
291: ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
292: │                                 │
293: │   [KEY VISUAL]      [TEXT]      │
294: │   (left 40%)     (right 60%)   │
295: │                                 │
296: │   Photo/diagram   2-4 words    │
297: │   or icon        bold font     │
298: │                                 │
299: └─────────────────────────────────┘
300: ```
301: 
302: **Two-segment layout**: Key visual on the left, concept/text on the right. This follows natural left-to-right reading flow. The photorealistic image draws the eye, then the text delivers the hook.
303: 
304: **Alternative layouts** (use sparingly):
305: - **Center composition**: Key visual centered with text above — for solo dramatic reveals
306: - **Split screen**: Left vs Right comparison — for "X vs Y" titles
307: - **Environmental**: Key visual tiny in a massive diagram — for scale/complexity
308: 
309: ### Color Rules
310: 
311: | Element | Color | Hex | Usage |
312: |---------|-------|-----|-------|
313: | Text (primary) | Bold Black | #000000–#1A1A1A | Default text color on white/light backgrounds |
314: | Text (alternate) | Deep Blue | #003366 | For emphasis or secondary headings |
315: | Text (accent) | Red | #FF0000 | Danger/urgency-related thumbnails |
316: | Background | White/Off-White | #FFFFFF–#F5F5F5 | Whiteboard canvas — clean and bright |
317: | Background (alt) | Light Gray | #EEEEEE | Subtle depth without distraction |
318: | Key visual | Photorealistic | N/A | Full-color product photos, diagrams, icons |
319: | Accent elements | Bright Orange | #FF6600 | Highlights, arrows, annotations |
320: | Accent elements | Cyan | #00FFFF | Technology, data, futuristic themes |

322: ### Whiteboard Thumbnail Composition Rules
323: 
324: The thumbnail must follow the clean whiteboard explainer aesthetic. Use these composition guidelines:
325: 
326: | Element | Rule | Example |
327: |---------|------|---------|
328: | Background | White or light, clean canvas | Plain white with subtle texture |
329: | Text | 2–4 words in bold handwritten font (Patrick Hand or Impact) | "EVERY", "HOW", "EXPLAINED", "WORST" |
330: | Key Visual | ONE photorealistic image or icon, high contrast | CPU photo, planet diagram, historical artifact |
331: | Layout | High contrast between text and visual | Bold dark text on white, vivid image beside it |
332: | Annotations | Hand-drawn arrows, circles, or underlines for emphasis | Arrow pointing from text to visual |
333: 
334: ### Font Style
335: 
336: - **Type**: Handwritten / marker style (Patrick Hand, Permanent Marker, or Impact for emphasis)
337: - **Weight**: Extra bold — strokes should be thick and readable
338: - **Case**: ALL CAPS always
339: - **Size**: Text should fill 30–50% of the thumbnail's width
340: - **Color**: Black (#000000) or Dark Blue (#003366) with optional highlight/underline for emphasis
341: - **Rotation**: Slight rotation (2–5°) adds energy and hand-drawn feel
342: - **No serif fonts, no thin sans-serif fonts** — it must feel like handwriting on a whiteboard
343: 
344: ### Core Emotions to Target
345: 
346: Every thumbnail must trigger ONE of these emotions:
347: 
348: 1. **Curiosity**: "Wait, how does that work?" → explanations, mechanisms, systems
349: 2. **Fascination**: "I never thought about that!" → surprising connections, hidden details
350: 3. **Shock**: "No way, really?" → surprising facts, statistics, reveals
351: 4. **Morbid Fascination**: "I shouldn't want to know but I do" → worst disasters, punishments, failures
352: 5. **Awe**: "That's incredible" → scale, engineering marvels, cosmic phenomena

356: **Example 1 — "What Dying on Every Planet Would Be Like" (ThePaintExplainer, 12M)**
357: - Clean white background with planet icons arranged in a row
358: - One photorealistic planet image as the focal point
359: - Text: "EVERY PLANET" in bold handwritten font
360: - Arrows and annotations pointing to different planets
361: - **Why it works**: The systematic layout implies comprehensive coverage. The viewer NEEDS to know what happens on each one. The whiteboard style makes complex info feel accessible.
362: 
363: **Example 2 — "Every Major Human Mistake That Changed History" (ThePaintExplainer, 7.5M)**
364: - White canvas with timeline-style layout
365: - Photorealistic historical images as visual anchors
366: - Bold text: "EVERY MISTAKE" with hand-drawn underline
367: - Red accent marks for emphasis
368: - **Why it works**: The word "EVERY" implies completeness — viewers want to see the full list. "Mistake" implies consequences. The clean layout makes it feel well-researched.

431: ## 8. Title A/B Testing Framework
432: 
433: ### Write 3 Variations for Every Video
434: 
435: Never publish the first title you think of. Always generate at least 3 variations using different psychological triggers.
436: 
437: ### The Three Variation Types
438: 
439: **Version A — Curiosity Gap**
440: - Creates an unanswered question the viewer MUST resolve
441: - Uses words like: hidden, secret, real reason, nobody talks about, actually
442: - Example: "The Hidden Reason Your Wi-Fi Is So Slow"
443: - **Best for**: Technology, mystery, counter-intuitive topics
444: 
445: **Version B — Direct Challenge**
446: - Challenges the viewer's assumptions or current behavior
447: - Uses words like: wrong, actually, really, think, believe
448: - Example: "You've Been Using Your Computer Wrong This Whole Time"
449: - **Best for**: Tech literacy, paradigm shifts, contrarian takes
450: 
451: **Version C — Specificity / Comprehensiveness**
452: - Uses specific scope, named entities, or "every" framing
453: - Uses words like: every, complete, all, from [X] to [Y], explained
454: - Example: "Every Type of Computer Memory Explained — From RAM to SSD"
455: - **Best for**: Science, technology, history, how-things-work topics

461: | Criteria | Weight | Description |
462: |----------|--------|-------------|
463: | Curiosity Strength | 5x | How badly do you NEED to click? |
464: | Emotional Trigger | 4x | Does it make you feel something? |
465: | Specificity | 3x | Is it concrete or vague? |
466: | Uniqueness | 3x | Does it sound different from existing videos? |
467: | Thumbnail Synergy | 4x | Does it pair well with a thumbnail concept? |
468: | Mobile Readability | 2x | Is it scannable on a phone screen? |
469: | Length | 1x | Under 60 characters is ideal; under 50 is better |

509: | Too broad | "The History of Everything" | No specificity = no curiosity gap |

512: 
513: **BAD framing** → **GOOD framing**:
514: 
515: | ❌ Dead Framing | ✅ Alive Framing | Why |
516: |-----------------|-------------------|-----|
517: | "The Mere Exposure Effect Explained" | "Why Your Brain Trusts Faces You've Seen Before" | Personal + specific |
518: | "How Earthquakes Work" | "What the First 60 Seconds of a Mega-Earthquake Feel Like" | Experiential + timeframe |
519: | "The Science of Sleep" | "Why Humans Used to Sleep Twice a Night" | Unexpected fact + ancient |
520: | "Nuclear Energy Explained" | "How a Nuclear Reactor Actually Works — Step by Step" | Demystification + process |
521: | "The Water Cycle" | "What Happens If Every River on Earth Dried Up Tomorrow" | Apocalyptic + urgency |
522: | "Evolution of Computer Processors" | "Every CPU Generation Explained — From 1971 to Now" | Comprehensive + timeline |
523: | "The Psychology of Fear" | "The Terrifying Reason You Freeze When You Should Run" | Terror + personal behavior |
524: | "Climate Change Effects" | "The 5 Places That Will Be Underwater by 2050" | Specificity + near-future dread |

526: ### Content Traps to Avoid
527: 
528: 1. **The "Interesting Fact" Trap**: Topics that are mildly interesting but not click-worthy. "Did you know dolphins sleep with one eye open?" — interesting at a dinner party, won't get clicks.
529: 
530: 2. **The "Trending News" Trap**: Current events get views for 48 hours then die. Your video takes 3 days to produce. By the time it's done, nobody cares.
531: 
532: 3. **The "Personal Interest" Trap**: YOU find quantum physics fascinating. Your 18–34 year old audience finds "How Quantum Computers Actually Work" fascinating. These are not the same thing. Always serve the audience, not yourself.
533: 
534: 4. **The "Sequel" Trap**: "Part 2" gets 30–70% fewer views than Part 1. Every video must stand alone. If you want to cover more, find a NEW angle with a new title.

536: 5. **The "Already Perfect" Trap**: If Kurzgesagt already made the definitive version with 20M views, you need a meaningfully DIFFERENT angle or you're competing for scraps.
